Thank you to the board and commissioners for the opportunity to speak today.
I am here as program manager of Buildup Saskatoon, which is a social enterprise and a program of client development.
We've recently completed a research project in collaboration with the city, the police service and the center for the study of co-ops at the University of Saskatoon.
And we are happy to basically share some of the information that came from not research report.
And we'd like to thank the city and the police service for their collaboration in this effort to gather the data required for this research report.
So a little bit about who we are and what we do.
We are essentially a program that functions as a reintegration and intervention service, essentially for folks transitioning out of the justice system.
Both federally and provincially, as well as folks looking to leave the gang lifestyle.
We've existed for a few years. We began in collaboration with straight up and are modeled basically on equipment housing model was inspiration.
And the housing first approach, we thought, well, what could we do in terms of employment? Could we create an employment first approach for a program?
So I'll build up Saskatoon, basically, is modeled on the idea that for folks who have made a decision to try to get their life back on the street narrow.
There needs to be an outlet for them to pursue that path.
We have found that many people, after spending some time in corrections, there are no opportunities or very limited opportunities when folks transition out.

They may have all the best intentions in the world, but ultimately the record functions as a shackle around their ankles and they're unable to really pursue any kind of meaningful path to get themselves back on track.
So as an organization, we seek to support train and employ folks who have justice background and we do so through construction.
So we function as a social enterprise that provides tailored supports for individuals who are coming out of these challenging situations.
And that can range from anything from helping them get a driver's license to securing independent housing, managing their addictions or their justice obligations.
And even up to including getting their kids back into their custody. So while doing this, we're also working on construction training and skill building.

Helping to build their employability skills, social skills, with the hope that eventually they may have an opportunity to transition into mainstream employment once they've gained a certain degree of stability.
We have felt that our opportunity to kind of amplify what we do in the community.
Can we turn inward and look at our core communities where there's the greatest need and can we focus our services in these communities?

So we have taken to doing a lot of work in affordable housing, apartment turn around using the skills of our folks in our program to actually help address a multitude of different issues that exist in our core communities.
We also offer below market construction services to our CBO partners and other affordable housing providers.

And we felt that in order for us to really accurately tell our story, a partnership with the University through a research project would be a great way to tell our story from a sand non bias perspective from a third party.
You can evaluate what we do both quantitatively and qualitatively.
And recently in the release of this project we're happy to say that using a relatively narrow scope that really was provided to us with a lot of help from Superintendent Pringles.
So I'd like to thank very much for his support and important contributions.
We were able to evaluate the cost to both the police and corrections of the interactions that many of our folks have experienced in the past.
Whether that's contact with police, incarceration, the cost to victim services, court costs, things of that nature.
And we're able to essentially evaluate, are we able to demonstrate a return on investment through our program and can we demonstrate cost savings to the community?
If a program like ours is supported and potentially expanded, and thanks to the hard work of the folks at the University and the research team,
we're able to demonstrate with a relatively narrow focus of data that we can, in fact, save both the taxpayer and the government, multiple levels.
Funding and money from the ability to keep folks out of the system.
One of our crew members employed for a year and supported is approximately half the cost of incarcerating them.
So we are hoping to use this research data to leverage kind of what we're doing and to help better tell the story to our municipal, provincial federal partners and our community partners.
To hopefully continue to invest in supporting these folks and creating opportunities rather than necessarily defaulting to the incarceration.
